## My Reasoning

I've been farming this land in Quzhou my whole life. My father grew wheat and maize, and so did his father. The soil here on the North China Plain is good for these two crops and the rotation works — wheat in winter, maize in summer, same fields. I don't need to think hard about this. Everyone around me does it, the grain station takes both, and I know exactly what each crop needs.

I have about 10 mu under cultivation. I could try cotton or vegetables, but the market is unreliable and I don't have the contacts or irrigation setup for vegetables. Wheat and maize are stable. The government also sets floor prices for grain, so I won't lose badly.

For wheat I'll use the Jimai variety the seed station sells — it yields well and I've used it before. I'll do rotary tillage after maize harvest to break up the stubble, then apply base fertilizer before planting. I'll top-dress urea at jointing. I irrigate three times: once at sowing if the soil is dry, once at jointing, once at heading. Stripe rust and aphids are my main worries, so two pesticide sprays.

For maize I go straight into the wheat stubble — no-till saves me money on fuel and I don't have time to plow before rain comes. I use a郑单958-type hybrid, everyone uses it. Maize gets summer rain so I only irrigate once if July is dry. Two pesticide passes: one herbicide early, one for corn borer.

My nitrogen is on the heavier side — I'd rather not lose yield. I know the extension office says I apply too much, but my neighbor who cut back had a bad year and I'm not willing to risk it.
